content: To determine whether an argument is deductively valid, especially when negation is involved, begin by translating all informal statements into precise formal logical notation. Explicitly represent universal quantifiers (∀, "all," "every"), existential quantifiers (∃, "some," "infrequent user"), and predicates, paying close attention to how negation (e.g., "not," "infrequent") modifies quantifier scope—such as turning ∀x P(x) into ∃x ¬P(x) or altering predicate membership. Once formalized, systematically check for counterexamples by asking: "Could there be a scenario where all premises are true, but the conclusion is false, particularly when negation introduces ambiguity between universal and existential claims?" Focus on cases where negation might misalign quantifiers (e.g., negating a universal claim may allow exceptions that invalidate the conclusion). If any such counterexample exists, the argument is invalid; otherwise, it is valid. This structured approach ensures consistent distinction between valid syllogisms and formal fallacies involving negation.
